title: [Vantage Point] Corruption floods Philippine economy
summary: What makes the corruption scandal so damaging is that it has crippled the state’s primary tool for counteracting economic headwinds

blocks.text: The flood-control scandal is no longer simply about questionable contracts, missing dikes, or billions of pesos siphoned from the national treasury. Its economic fallout is now visible across the real economy: public works have ground to a halt, infrastructure spending is contracting, and legitimate builders are drowning in unpaid bills. The Philippines is discovering the hard way that corruption continues to exact a crushing toll long after the stolen cash has vanished.
Corruption inevitably presents two separate bills to the Filipino taxpayer.

The first arrives when public money leaks into inflated project bids, shoddy materials, and ghost drainage structures that exist solely on paper. The second arrives much later, when the bureaucratic machinery seizes up.

Legitimate public works stall, honest contractors wait endlessly for payments, and daily-wage laborers wonder how they will feed their families. The first bill is a brazen theft that sparks moral outrage. The second is a silent administrative breakdown that can steadily undermine an entire national economy.
The Philippines is now confronting that second bill, and the economic data have become impossible to brush aside.

Economic growth slowed to a sluggish 2.1% in the third quarter of 2026, down sharply from 4% a year earlier. Government construction plunged by 15.1%, extending a painful contraction across six straight quarters. Total construction activity slid 4%, while overall capital investment dipped 0.2%. These are not merely abstract figures in an academic report. They reveal an economy losing vital momentum at the precise moment robust public investment should be shielding households from expensive borrowing costs and sluggish consumer demand.

blocks.caption: Source: Philippine Statistics Authority; GDP growth, year on year.

blocks.text: More alarming is the steep contraction documented in the government’s own accounting ledgers.

During the first eight months of 2026, spending on infrastructure and capital outlays fell to P522 billion, down from P798.4 billion during the same period last year. That reflects a massive drop of P276.4 billion, or 34.6%. While overall state disbursements rose, actual capital spending moved sharply in reverse, driven largely by paralyzing bottlenecks within the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

blocks.caption: Source: Department of Budget and Management; first eight months of each year. Decline: P276.4B (34.6%).

blocks.text: That P276.4-billion drop does not represent an estimate of stolen wealth. It simply captures the gap between two periods of state spending. Yet the real-world fallout is severe. Every peso withheld from an honest infrastructure project means cancelled work shifts, idled bulldozers, unpaid hardware suppliers, and delayed improvements to the country’s logistical backbone.

Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan has conceded that bottlenecks in project validation and disbursements have crippled project delivery. These disruptions severely hinder builders from meeting payroll, purchasing supplies, and bidding on new ventures. Lingering governance scandals and institutional uncertainty have chilled investor confidence across the board. (READ: [In This Economy] The Philippines has entered stagflation territory)

Here lies the insidious economic legacy of the flood-control scandal. What began as investigations into specific anomalies has exposed systemic frailties in how the state procures, verifies, and pays for civil works. Government agencies now find themselves attempting to identify irregular contracts while simultaneously trying to keep honest builders solvent.

Consider a reputable contractor who completed an honest road widening or drainage network months ago. He cannot collect his rightful progress billings because state auditors must run endless verification checks on paperwork. His commercial bank does not suspend interest charges while inspectors recheck measurements. His cement supplier still expects timely settlement. His equipment lessor demands payment, and his site workers still need their weekly pay. Eventually, an administrative delay in a regional budget office morphs into an existential cash crunch for an otherwise viable enterprise.

Multiply that predicament across hundreds of general contractors, subcontractors, quarries, steel fabricators, hauling services, and equipment rental firms. The financial damage quickly cascades downward. Small and medium enterprises suffer first and worst because they lack the deep financial reserves required to bankroll state infrastructure out of pocket.

Commercial lenders inevitably inherit part of the damage through non-performing loans, stretched credit facilities, and deteriorated borrower cash flows. While the financial system remains well-capitalized, the transmission mechanism is straightforward: when builders cannot collect from the state, banks face rising credit risks precisely when financing is already tight. (READ: [Vantage Point] Landbank’s P182-million belated retreat)

Legal accountability must proceed. On November 6, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla reported that 79 criminal cases involving flood-control projects valued at roughly P10.78 billion had reached the courts, with charges including plunder, malversation, and anti-graft violations. While that figure reflects total contract values under judicial review rather than verified stolen wealth, the legal reckoning is necessary.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Ombudsman’s presentation on November 6, 2026.

blocks.text: Yet while prosecutors assemble their dossiers, the economy absorbs the blow.

To be fair, corruption did not cause every economic headwind. Elevated power rates, persistent inflation, severe storm damage to agriculture, and high interest rates have all dampened expansion. Headline inflation hit 7.8% in October, while consumer spending rose only 2.4% in the third quarter. These external pressures are genuine.

What makes the governance scandal so damaging is that it has crippled the state’s primary tool for counteracting these headwinds. Rather than injecting vital stimulus and creating local employment, public works programs remain snarled in fear and red tape. Bureaucrats now hesitate to approve routine disbursements lest they face subsequent graft charges, while abandoning oversight would invite renewed pillage.

The Marcos administration must urgently fix this operational impasse. It must establish a clean, swift mechanism to separate clean contracts from fraudulent ones, ensuring that verified work receives payment without delay. Full public disclosure of contract sums, physical progress, and actual disbursements must become mandatory.

The true cost of corruption cannot be measured solely by the assets prosecutors recover or the prison terms handed down. It encompasses idled projects, bankrupt suppliers, lost wages, and squandered opportunities.
The cruelest irony is that ordinary citizens — those who never saw a centavo of illicit gain — are left footing the ultimate bill. – Rappler.com
